frameworks.name: 3A Reframing Framework
frameworks.definition: A three-step sales objection-handling sequence: Acknowledge (restate the prospect's concern to build rapport and buy thinking time), Associate (link the prospect's question or objection to behaviors of the best-performing customers), then Ask (redirect with a targeted question rather than answering the original objection directly).

frameworks.name: Straw Man Association
frameworks.definition: A technique for delivering a harsh truth in a sales call without insulting the prospect directly: create a third-party foil (a recent customer, a named success story, or an authority figure like the CEO) whose situation mirrors the prospect's, then address the tough truth to the foil rather than to the prospect.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the single highest-leverage differentiator between top-performing salespeople and average ones is the frequency with which they ask for the sale: the best closers make more close attempts than anyone else. The problem is that asking repeatedly the wrong way destroys rapport, so the mechanism of asking must maintain rapport throughout, enabling repeated asks without prospect resistance.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: best closers make the most asks
conditions: high-touch sales context
multi-attempt closing situations
claims.mechanism: Asking in a rapport-preserving manner keeps the prospect emotionally open, allowing the salesperson to ask as many times as needed without the prospect disengaging.
bounded_by: Asking repeatedly without rapport maintenance causes prospects to disengage or become hostile

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the person asking the questions in a sales conversation controls the conversation: as soon as the salesperson begins answering the prospect's questions, the prospect becomes judge, jury, and executioner of whether those answers are sufficient, putting the salesperson on defense.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: the person asking the questions is the one who's in control
conditions: any sales conversation format: in-person, phone, Zoom, from stage
claims.mechanism: Whoever asks questions directs the conversation topic and evaluation criteria; answering questions cedes that directional power to the prospect and allows the prospect to declare an answer insufficient.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a prospect believes almost nothing that the salesperson tells them and almost everything that they themselves say. Therefore the goal of a sales conversation is not to tell prospects they are a good fit, but to ask questions that lead prospects to declare themselves a good fit.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: breadcrumb them to the logical solution
conditions: any sales context where the prospect is evaluating a purchase
claims.mechanism: Self-generated conclusions carry higher credibility than externally asserted claims because of the source-credibility asymmetry between the prospect trusting themselves vs. trusting a salesperson with an obvious incentive.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that asking the question do you have any questions? is among the worst things a salesperson can do, because it explicitly invites objections and hands control of the conversation to the prospect.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: the worst question to ever ask in sales
conditions: any sales call or pitch

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that in service business sales, the people doing the selling are frequently less technically knowledgeable than those delivering the service, and that attempting to answer technical prospect questions from a position of insufficient knowledge systematically sets salespeople up to lose the sale.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: they basically set themselves up for failure
conditions: service businesses where delivery personnel differ from sales personnel

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a salesperson can never win a sale by winning an argument with a prospect: when both parties argue, both lose, and for the salesperson, losing the argument means losing the sale. The goal is to help the prospect change their own mind through questions, not to defeat their position through logic.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: you never win a sale by winning an argument
conditions: any sales conversation involving prospect objections or resistance

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that using the Acknowledge-Associate-Ask (3A) reframing sequence before entering a close allows a salesperson to say almost anything and maintain rapport, because the prospect feels heard and validated. Skipping the reframe makes the close feel combative and reduces close rate even when the close language itself is correct.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: if you preface with this, you can say almost anything
conditions: sales calls with repeated close attempts
offers from $100 to $1M+
claims.mechanism: Acknowledgment signals active listening; association elevates the prospect's self-perception as a rational or successful buyer type; together they restore emotional neutrality so the prospect can evaluate the next ask without defensive framing.

numbers.axis: offer price range where reframing has been validated

bounded_by: Requires genuine qualification of the prospect; unethical to use on unqualified prospects who cannot get a good result

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the Association step of the 3A framework is especially powerful because it assigns the prospect a positive label (smart, rational, family-oriented) which the prospect then feels motivated to live up to. This label can be recalled at the close to pair the prospect's stated identity with the reason to buy.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: it gives the prospect a label to then live up to
conditions: sales calls long enough to establish rapport before close
claims.mechanism: Identity labels create consistency pressure: once a prospect accepts the label (smart person, family man), they are motivated to act consistently with it. The close can pair the label to the product to create an identity-aligned reason to buy.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that salespeople should treat every prospect statement or objection not as a deal-ender requiring a definitive answer, but as an invitation to ask further questions. Beginners treat objections as final statements and stop; experienced closers treat them as openings for more questions that keep the prospect in the sale.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: beginners will take a statement like that and think, oh, I guess they're not going to buy
conditions: any sales conversation with objections or hesitation

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that two behaviors constitute unethical selling: (1) selling to an unqualified prospect by implying they will get results when they are not actually qualified, and (2) failing to ask persistently and clearly when the prospect is genuinely qualified. For qualified prospects, the salesperson has an ethical obligation to ask as many times as necessary.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: you have the ethical obligation to ask as many times as easily possible
conditions: prospect is genuinely qualified for the product or service
product will deliver results for this prospect
bounded_by: Ethical obligation to ask repeatedly applies only to qualified prospects; selling to an unqualified prospect is unethical regardless of the technique used

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that straw man associations are especially important when the salesperson needs to break a prospect's false belief or deliver a harsh truth. Using a third-party foil (a past customer, a recent conversation subject, or an authority figure) allows the salesperson to say something blunt without the prospect feeling directly attacked or insulted.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prospect holds a clearly flawed belief that must be corrected to close
salesperson has less age or authority than prospect (e.g., 22-year-old selling to a 45-year-old $10M business owner)
claims.mechanism: The foil creates a neutral third party: the salesperson addresses the harsh truth to the foil, not the prospect, removing the interpersonal sting of direct contradiction while still delivering the corrective message.
bounded_by: Age or authority differentials (e.g., young salesperson to established senior buyer) reduce effectiveness of self-referential authority appeals; straw men are the workaround in those cases

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that retaining a physically curious posture and tone (e.g., the hmm pause before responding) materially affects close outcomes even on phone calls where the prospect cannot see the salesperson, because posture and emotional state alter vocal tone, which the prospect detects.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: your tone will change based on how you're standing
conditions: phone and Zoom sales calls
claims.mechanism: Physical posture and facial expression modulate vocal tone in ways the listener perceives subconsciously; a mirror during phone calls allows the salesperson to monitor and correct their own expression in real time.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that experienced salespeople should never be surprised by any question or objection a prospect raises, because they have had the same conversation hundreds or thousands of times. If a prospect can surprise a seasoned rep, it is a training and preparation failure, not an exceptional situation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: the fact that somebody could surprise you is ridiculous
conditions: salespeople with substantial call volume in a specific offer or market

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a salesperson's primary objective is to make the prospect feel right, not to prove that the salesperson is right. Winning the logical argument but losing rapport causes the prospect to disengage, and the sale is lost even when the salesperson's position is objectively correct.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: you don't close sales by being right, you close sales by making the prospect right
conditions: any sales context with prospect objections

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the question what are you most afraid of? is the fastest path to the core objection when a prospect is already deep into the sales conversation. Earlier in the conversation, questions like what is your main concern? or what are the variables you are using to make this decision? are more appropriate for triage.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: what are you afraid of gets you to the heart of the issue as fast as possible
conditions: prospect is far along in the sales conversation and has not committed
earlier in the conversation: use triage questions first
bounded_by: Asking what are you afraid of too early, before rapport is established, will cause the prospect to disengage

examples.text: A prospect asks how many certifications the trainers have. Instead of answering and letting the prospect judge whether the answer is sufficient, the salesperson using the 3A framework says: So you're curious about certifications? That's a great question, it shows you're a really rational person making a serious decision here, which is amazing. Then the salesperson attacks the frame: which certification are you looking for specifically? Most prospects have never been asked this follow-up question and do not actually know which certification they want. They say I don't know, at which point the salesperson can say let me tell you what we have and why. If the prospect names a specific certification the company does not hold, the salesperson asks why those certifications specifically? and then reframes the company's certifications relative to the named ones rather than being caught flat-footed with a no.

A wealth management salesperson opened with: Oh, that's amazing. 90% of the clients we shift over already have a wealth advisor, so it means you already know how a lot of these things work, which means you'll be up the learning curve. Alex Hormozi, who had entered the conversation intending to exit it as quickly as possible, reported that this association reframe caught him completely off guard: he had presented what he thought was a disqualifying condition (existing advisor) and the salesperson immediately reframed it as a positive qualification marker shared by the best buyers. Hormozi did not ultimately buy from that salesperson, but credited this moment as the source of his systematic adoption of the association technique across his own sales operations.

Alex Hormozi recounts walking the sales floor and hearing a salesperson ask a weakly committed prospect so you coming? and receiving a non-committal yeah. Hormozi took the phone and asked dude, what are you afraid of? directly, cutting immediately to the core concern rather than accepting the vague response. This example illustrates the use of the what are you afraid of question at the late stage of a sale to surface the actual objection rather than letting the prospect drift out.

A salesperson who says I need to think about it is met with: Totally understand. What are the main things you're considering? What are the variables you are using to make the decision? What's your main concern? What are you most afraid of having happen? What would make this a no? And: What would it take for you to say yes? Alex Hormozi presents this sequence as a demonstration of using questions to stay in the sale rather than accepting a non-commitment as a conversation-ender.

For the I need to talk to my spouse objection, the 3A sequence runs: Totally understand, I think it's really sensible that you'd want to talk to your spouse, super fair. Just so I understand out of curiosity, what parts do you think they wouldn't like? What parts do you think they would disagree with? The conversation has now moved from an exit (I have to check with my spouse) back into the active sale, with the prospect naming specific objections that the salesperson can now address directly.

A prospect who says the timing is off right now is met with: Totally understand. Timing is kind of tough for you right now. I think it's smart that you're already thinking about implementation. Our biggest success stories are actually people who think through the process the same way you are right now. So what would make it a good time? This example illustrates all three 3A steps in sequence: Acknowledge (timing tough), Associate (biggest success stories think this way too), Ask (what would make it a good time).

practices.text: Train the question do you have any questions? out of every salesperson on your team.
Place a mirror next to the phone during sales calls so you can monitor your own facial expression in real time.
Put a sticky note above the camera or wherever you look during selling that reads keep the human number one as a frame for maintaining prospect-first orientation.
When a prospect gives a weak or vague non-commitment late in the sale, ask what are you afraid of? to surface the real objection rather than accepting the soft no.

When answering a question that would require technical knowledge the salesperson lacks, use the mechanic analogy: it would be unethical for me to tell you what is wrong with your car without looking under the hood first; we can give you much better answers once we have started working together.
When you cannot directly answer a prospect's question, always ask more questions about the question rather than attempting to construct an answer you do not actually have.

When associating a prospect's objection to successful-customer behavior, store the positive label you assign them and bring it back at the close to pair their stated identity with the buying decision.
